Chance Garton Sacred Math and the Septenary Cipher Marty Leeds walks through the septenary cipher, his seven based gematria system, showing how the word seven itself hides the numbers seven and twenty two, the classic fraction for approximating pi. He ties that into the tarot's structure: twenty two Major Arcana cards, fifty six Minor Arcana split into four suits of fourteen, mirroring the fourteen phalanges on a hand, for seventy eight cards total, which also equals one through twelve summed, the twelve houses of astrology. Even earth, air, water and fire, the elements of the astrological wheel, sum to seventy eight again, reinforcing what he calls a self referential, mathematically encoded system, not coincidence. The Fool, the Magician and the Holy Fool Mario reads the Fool and Magician as chaos becoming order, echoing the primordial jumble of elements in Ovid's Metamorphoses before a world axis separates heaven from earth. Marty adds that Genesis performs the same split, with earth, air, water and fire present before God says let there be light, a phrase whose gematria equals seventy two, the same value as Lord Jesus Christ. The Fool sums to thirty, but adding holy brings it to forty two, the Magician's number, and Marty notes those same digits begin the unfolding of pi, three one four. Even the Fool's own divisors, he says, reduce mathematically straight to Lord Jesus Christ. Stars and Constellations Hidden in the Cards Several cards double as star charts for the two guests. The Chariot's motionless charioteer is an unmoved mover whose wheels sit in the waters of heaven, which Marty links to the constellation Auriga while Mario traces the glyph for seven to the seven stars of Ursa Major wheeling around the pole. The Hermit stands atop a world mountain, his lantern and closed eyes pointing toward Polaris, with Mario connecting the card's Virgo rulership to Mercury. Marty argues the Fool himself is Orion, walking obliviously toward a ledge while Canis Major, the barking dog, marks Sirius, the star that signals where the sun rises each December twenty fifth. Mercury, the World Axis and Sacred Geometry Mercury keeps resurfacing as the one planet with no zodiacal opposite, which Marty reads as its role uniting opposites, the alchemical coincidentia oppositorum; its eighty eight day orbit divided by twenty eight phalanges of the hand approximates pi again. Mario frames Mercury, the Hermit's staff and the Magician's raised and lowered hands as the same Axis Mundi, the spinal column and world pillar connecting above and below. That geometry resolves into the cube, Marty's stand in for Kabbalah, with Jesus and the Magician reducing through gematria to four thirty two, doubling to four thousand three twenty, the degrees of two cubes, alongside the six six six drawn from Jesus's value. The Fool's Journey as Human Awakening Beyond the numbers, both guests treat the Fool as everyman, someone who, like the rest of us, simply hasn't recognized his own divine spark yet. Chance frames it as all people being peepholes of God, each ego a temporary window onto something infinite. Mario reads the Fool's eagle topped bag as Scorpio's sexual energy, either weighing him down or transformed, Phoenix like, into enlightenment, noting he's the only figure in the deck shown walking, traveling lightly rather than burdened. Chance shares his own experience of choosing, during mystical states, to return to ordinary life, framing the Fool's descent from the mountain as a forgetting on the road back to wholeness.

A Genre With A Formula What Tartaria really is, Chance argues, is a genre with a repeatable formula: show a photo of an 1800s building, claim the population was too small, the logistics impossible and the construction record missing, read a line off Wikipedia, project incredulity for twenty minutes and conclude it must be Tartaria. He tells Joel and Aurassimus that most of the big channels launched in 2025 and 2026 are full AI productions, and he screen shares a Tartaria Instagram post that had pasted the floating city from the video game BioShock Infinite over a Chicago World's Fair photograph. Inside The Insane Asylums Chance's favorite work in the project is on the 1800s insane asylums, the long batwing buildings that Tartaria videos call repurposed old world castles or extermination camps for people who remembered. Across roughly seven hours of content he presents construction records for ten or twelve of them, down to receipt books for the masons and the steam power, most of it pulled from archive.org and state legislature minutes. In Missouri, he found, lawmakers resisted building one until the governor took his own life. The design came from alienists and their philosophy of environmental determinism: fresh air, clean food, nature and space. Chicago, The Fair And The Fire Two load bearing pillars of the theory sit in Chicago. Chance says the World's Fair buildings were framed in wood and some steel, then molded in a plaster called staff to imitate carved stone, essentially a movie set, and that a surviving book of blueprints is named in Howdy McCoskey's own book after McCoskey claims none exist. He ballparks the cost at 600 to 800 million dollars in modern money. On the Great Chicago Fire he points to wooden sidewalks, tar coated wood block streets, one inch of rain from July to October, and fires across Wisconsin and Michigan the same day. Donnelly, Atlantis And The Sacred Cow Researching the fire led Chance to Ignatius Donnelly, whom he calls the modern origin of the whole lost civilization and cataclysm genre. In Ragnarok, written about twelve years after 1871, Donnelly blamed the Chicago and Peshtigo fires on fragments of Biela's Comet, which astronomers had watched split in two in 1846. Chance's objection is that the comet does not come around until late November while those fires burned in early October. Donnelly's Atlantis, he argues, seeded Blavatsky and Steiner, and he reads Plato's Atlantis as allegory: a traditionalist society and a progressive proto Athens destroying each other.

Dylan Saccoccio Mythological Imperialism Dylan traces the name Jason back through Etruscan Hason and Celtic Esus to a bronze mirror inscribed HEASUN, arguing the story reached Greece rather than starting there. Etruscan city states held their own treasuries at Delphi, the Colchian dragon from this same myth still rides the Alfa Romeo crest, and the tombs and inscriptions across ancient Italy are non-Greek down to the paintings. The claim isn't that the Greeks invented nothing, it's that they inherited a Golden Fleece story from an older Italian priesthood and passed it off as their own. The Manuscript Gap The oldest complete Argonautica comes from Apollonius of Rhodes in the third century BC, a thousand years after the voyage supposedly happened, and the so-called Orphic Argonautica, once circulated as far older, is a fifteenth-century Renaissance forgery exposed by its own late Greek vocabulary. Homer and Hesiod mention Jason centuries earlier as though their audience already knew the story, but no surviving text tells it in full until long after those passing references. A physical fragment at Delphi, dated to around 480 BC, is the oldest artifact that might show the myth in Greece, and even that identification rests on guesswork. Astrotheology of the Golden Fleece The oldest surviving description of Jason's destination places it where the rays of the sun rest in a golden storeroom, Medea escapes in a chariot drawn by her grandfather Helios, and the fleece itself hangs in a grove sacred to Ares, the same root behind Aries, the ram, and the Lamb of God. Jason's upbringing by the foster parent Chiron echoes Moses, Dionysus, and Christ, and the Argo constellation is missing its stern, the exact detail the myth explains by having it sheared off at the Clashing Rocks. Yesun and the Priesthood's Favorite Title In the Greek of Matthew 1:21, the name rendered "Jesus" is closer to Yesun, sharing a root with Kyrios and Kiros, the same title behind the historical King Cyrus and the Curetes, the priests who guarded the infant Zeus. Dylan and Chance argue this isn't wordplay for its own sake, it's the same divine-son title recycled onto a different figure in a different tradition. Myth as a Deed to Someone Else's Land Alexander's own historians told the Armenians they were long-lost Greeks descended from the Argonaut Armenus, Strabo records a temple to Jason built by Alexander's top general, and Pindar's Pythian Four uses Medea's prophecy to hand a living king a mythological deed to a Libyan colony. Every version follows the same shape: claim ancestral kinship with a place first, and the conquest that follows reads as a homecoming instead of a hostile taking. Once you see the template, Chance and Dylan argue, you start seeing it everywhere in history.

Who Benefited From the Great Chicago Fire? The Verdict: Firebombing, Arson & the Real Chicago Conspiracy This document wasn't really intended for wide public consumption as a way to sell a story. It's just a document where they're counting the beans about what they lost. Chance Garton The exterior walls are basically like chimneys with houses in the middle. Chance Garton If the fire was some kind of clandestine operation to erase all the evidence of the old world architecture in Chicago, why would so much of that architecture remain standing? Chance Garton The historical record shows the exact opposite. A wooden city with stone facades, Chicago style construction, balloon framing. Chance Garton While brick and limestone might not be flammable in and of themselves, when you cook them long enough in a structural fire of wooden framed buildings, these materials are going to fall apart. Chance Garton Nobody needs to start the great fire. They just keep the fire department weak and incompetent in their leadership until eventually a big enough fire happens. Chance Garton They didn't hand out food. They didn't help build shelter. In other words, they were not really there to help. They were just there to guard the assets of the rich people. Chance Garton The powerful of the city converted this catastrophe into consolidation of power, and they did it really fast, in less than 90 days, and in broad daylight. Chance Garton The Water Tower That Survived The sharpest objection here is architectural. If the 1871 fire was a bombing run meant to erase old world buildings, why does so much grand stone still stand? William W. Boyington's Water Tower, finished in 1869 out of Joliet limestone, came through in full glory while its neighbors fell, and Oscar Wilde disliked it enough to call it a castellated monstrosity with pepper boxes stuck all over it in 1882. Old St. Patrick's from 1856, the Henry B. Clarke House from 1836, and Holy Family all survived. The Sherman House was rebuilt bigger, and the fire took only about a third of the city. A City Framed In Pine Chicago invented the building method that fed the fire. George Washington Snow framed a warehouse without hand cut joints in 1832, and a couple of years later the carpenter Augustine Taylor nailed St. Mary's Church together from light 2x4s for about $400, a technique mocked as balloon construction until it became known instead as Chicago construction. Its wall cavities ran from foundation to roof with no fire stops. Add roughly 60,000 buildings that were about 90 percent wood, 561 miles of raised plank sidewalk, 57 miles of tar coated wood block street, and one inch of rain from July to October. Nobody Left To Fight It The fire department was already broken before the first alarm sounded. In the six days before October 8, Chicago's roughly 185 to 219 firemen answered 27 alarms and worked 24 fires, then spent 14 to 17 hours on the Saturday night Red Flash fire that leveled four blocks of lumber yards and mills and cost a million dollars. Hook and Ladder Company 1 lost all of its apparatus, two steam engines were disabled, and Engine Company 6 reached the O'Leary barn after 22 hours of work and one hour of rest. Watchman Matthias Schaefer then misjudged the location by a mile, and the telegraph operator refused to correct the box. Rubble Without Bombs The Tartaria case leans on how much the ruins resemble Dresden after Allied incendiary bombing, and Chance grants the resemblance before explaining it. Nineteenth century mortar most likely lost its integrity somewhere around 600 to 800 degrees, while a fuel rich structural fire easily reaches 1,200, 1,400, even 2,000, so unbound brick simply collapsed into chaotic piles. Local Lemont limestone heated past 1,500 degrees becomes quicklime and crumbles to powder. The blurry roof edges offered as proof of hidden airships are halation, a known glass plate effect. Even the Tribune's fireproof 1869 headquarters burned, undone by paper, archives, and linseed oil ink. Who Cashed In Fastest The city's own 11th annual Board of Public Works report from July 1872 tallies about $200 million lost across 1,687 acres, names no cause, and the cause has stayed undetermined ever since. What followed is documented. Three days after the fire, Mayor Roswell Mason handed authority to Lieutenant General Philip Sheridan under effective martial law that guarded bank rubble instead of feeding anyone. Two days later he routed every relief dollar, five to ten million of it, to the private Chicago Relief and Aid Society, which closed its books with $600,000 unspent. Within 30 days Joseph Medill won the mayoralty by 46 points.

I'm just analyzing something that caught my eye. Chance Garton So what your grandpa told you, it's cool. It's a nice little family thing, but it doesn't mean anything. Chance Garton You have no idea about actual America and older America because you're not from any of these parts. You didn't grow up seeing the actual antiquity of America. Chance Garton So don't take this the wrong way, but you have to raise your standards, my guy. Dylan Saccoccio The Eyewitness Tartaria Never Had Every old world reset story runs into the same hole: if settlers walked into finished cities, somebody's ancestor would have said so, in a journal, a diary, a passed down story. A YouTuber named Logan, of the channel Luminary Lighthouse, thought he finally had that account when a viewer named Jack Crowley commented that his ancestor, commissioned a high mason in New York, guided seventy five people to a fully built town in Kansas in 1840, all granite, with a capital type building in the middle, and a hidden journal to prove it. That journal is never produced, never even mentioned on air. What Council Grove Actually Records Council Grove takes its name from an 1825 treaty made under John Quincy Adams, in which Osage chiefs guaranteed passage along the Santa Fe Trail for an eight hundred dollar payoff. Commissioner George Champlain Sibley wrote on August 5, 1825 that he suggested the name and had it carved into an oak, a tree whose bark closed over the letters before photography existed. Seth Hays, grandson of Daniel Boone, put up the first cabin in 1847. Old photographs at kansasmemory.gov show wood framed shops, a railroad depot in 1869, and brick only after the 1886 fire. No granite, no capitol. Two Crowleys, One Broken Line The records are not close. A Morris County cemetery survey lists JJ Crowley with the 47th New York Infantry; New York's own regimental roster shows Crowley, John, aged twenty three, mustered in as a private on February 27, 1865, which puts his birth near 1842, two years after the town he supposedly founded. Allen Crowley, 1822 to 1891, reached the area in the 1850s and appears in a 1921 local history only as one of the old settlers, holding no county office. A public family tree names JJ's father as James Crowley, so Allen was never his father, and the two lines look unrelated. The Cropped Encyclopedia Page Rather than check any of this, Logan screen shared a page from the 1912 Kansas Encyclopedia of State History with the right margin cut off, then read it aloud as calling Allen Crowley the pioneer of the Neosho Valley, dropping the words that made him one of the pioneers. In a private message he conceded the dates were all wrong and offered Allen as a substitute ancestor, yet never corrected it on stream, and the video swings back to JJ. He then recommended part two, where Jack recalls a dead coworker's Mormon diary describing a finished granite Salt Lake City, capitol included, though that capitol was not begun until 1912. Skepticism Without The Homework The verdict is not that official history is honest. Both hosts grant that westward expansion is mythologized, that the Osage were conned out of far more than the trail, that governments tell noble lies. The objection is the leap. Knowing some history is false does not license jumping to mud floods, empty cities, and a reset, especially when the whole case rests on a document nobody has seen and a story that changes between a Facebook comment and a live stream. The closing appeal to Logan is modest: post a retraction, because credibility is the only thing that outlasts the ratings.

Chance notes that the biggest problem with flat earth proponents is how easily they berate people who never had reason to question the globe, and Tamara calls the transition painful and gut wrenching. The Curvature Case In Court Much of the episode turns on a lawsuit. Tamara recounts Zen Garcia's fifteen thousand dollar challenge to demonstrate curvature with three repeatable, testable proofs. William Thompson believed he had done it, sued for the money, and lost, because he could not establish curvature beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law. She pairs that with Nathan Oakley's book Measured Flat, arguing that every practical measurement, plumb, level, elevation, latitude, longitude and the compass, is taken from a horizontal plane of reference. Chance plays along on air, pointing north, south, east and west, and she calls that a flat plane of reference. Water, Containers, And Ice Walls Tamara carries a keychain bubble level and says the horizon stays at eye level from beaches, planes and balloons rather than dropping away on both sides. Water, she argues, is always flat and level, takes the shape of whatever holds it, and cannot keep its position without containment, which is why she treats Antarctica's tall shoreline cliffs as the rim of an enclosure rather than an edge to fall off. Chance stresses nobody claims a pizza floating in space, and raises the firmament dome, quoting Marty Leeds that everything beyond it is metaphysical. Tamara likens open gas beside a vacuum to propane without a tank. Polaris, Tides, And Terminator Lines The pair run through solar system mechanics. Tamara says a lit ball should show a clean terminator line and equal day and night, that tides rise on both sides of the planet while fresh water ignores the moon, and that gravity cannot hold the moon at 238,000 miles while astronauts float 250 miles up. Her Polaris poem multiplies six trillion miles by 433 light years to mock the scale, and she invokes the inverse square law. She points to the Georgia Guidestones hole always framing Polaris, and to Mercury and Venus appearing at dusk and dawn, dismissing refraction as the answer given for everything. Steelmanning The Globe On Air Chance says he spent days trying to falsify his own position, treating pole to pole circumnavigation as the strongest test, and found stories and a few photographs but no receipts. He plays a TikTok using a sculpture, a fiber optic camera and a toy boat, calling it a flawed experiment because a tabletop cannot reach the vanishing point, while granting that ships really do appear to vanish from the bottom up. Chance Garton Seven Years In A Wheelchair Gillmore recounts a car accident and then a fall in 2003 that left her with a neurological disorder, extreme pain and years in a wheelchair. She describes trying nerve ablations, infusions and injections, then reaching outward to diets, detoxes, fasts, supplements, meditation, affirmations and binaural beats, and finding that none of it touched what she was living with. What stayed with her, she says, was noticing that her nerves would recover after a procedure while the underlying injury did not, and hearing doctors repeat that there was nothing more they could do for her. The Study That Sent Her Home She describes arriving at a medical study at a top hospital certain she was there to get her life back, wheeled in by a friend, set up on a gurney and connected to IVs, only to have the doctor review her chart and tell her she could not take part because they did not expect her to improve. She recounts arguing that this was her life, being treated outside the study anyway, and going home to no change. Lying there afterward, she says, a question about the placebo surfaced in her head and gave her a reason not to quit. Different Personalities, Different Illnesses The research that jolted her, Gillmore says, involved people with multiple personality disorder, including a reported case of a woman described as medically blind in some personalities and sighted in others, and cases where one personality carried an illness while another did not. That pushed her question away from whether trauma existed and toward why it seemed to land so unevenly, since she had noticed police and military people who had been through extreme events without becoming ill. Her working frame became ingredients, a specific combination rather than trauma on its own, and belief alone was not enough. The Guilt Underneath The Trauma The counterintuitive piece in her own case, Gillmore recounts, was survivors guilt. Working an early morning shift in California, she had been on the phone with colleagues in the trade towers on 9/11, could do nothing as it unfolded, then watched the footage replay for months and carried a suppressed sense that she should have died saving others. Erasmus worked from that damaged copy while assembling his Textus Receptus, and because its final six verses were missing he filled the gap by translating backward out of Jerome's Latin Vulgate. Erasmus left it out of his first two Greek editions because he could find it in no Greek manuscript, only in later Latin copies, and after being attacked by Stunica and the Archbishop of York he reportedly promised to include it if anyone produced a single Greek witness. One promptly appeared in Britain, the Codex Montfortianus, which scholars now widely regard as forged to win the argument. Saccoccio contends such timely discoveries were the rule, not the exception. His contention is that the Oriental origin story is an inversion: alphabets gain letters rather than lose them, and Hebrew and Phoenician, he says, have nothing to do with each other. The Moses's: A Plural Name Buried in Josephus's Greek The show's original claim is philological. Taylor noted that Josephus, Philo, Manetho, Diodorus, Orpheus and Strabo speak of the Moses, a plural, so books according to the Moses rather than by one man. Dylan shows the Greek himself: the termination iota omicron iota sigma, with omega and epsilon before the sigma, preceded by the article, reading closer to Moises or Muses than Moses, and apparently pluralized twice. He finds the same iota omicron iota sigma plural on Assyrians in the Chronicon Paschale, notes Josephus survives only as Greek minuscule copies from the ninth to eleventh centuries, and floats a medieval French hand, perhaps Avignon. Melissa Kupsch Spirit Precedes Form: The Vitalist Premise Chance opens by arguing that the physicalist view, that an object's qualities emerge from its material composition, is the most distorting precept of the Kali Yuga, and he points to the hard problem of consciousness, near death experiences, out of body travel and synchronicity as evidence that spirit precedes form. Melissa contends the medicine was widely used historically, then suppressed, and is now in a genuine resurgence. Taking the Whole Case, Not the Seven Minute Version Melissa describes how a homeopath takes a case: at least ninety minutes, compared with the roughly seven minutes she says an Australian bulk billed Medicare consultation allows from walking in to walking out with a prescription. She asks clients for a timeline from birth, even from the womb if the mother carried trauma, right up to the present, and says many people have never been asked that question. She calls the search for the origin point the never well since, and explains that a chronic pattern recurring in cycles signals, in her framework, something blocking the vital force rather than a discrete disease to be named. Resonance, Adaptation and the Story Underneath Kyle describes customers at his herb shop drawn to a wall of jars, pulling one down like a tarot card and asking what it is good for, then recognising themselves in his answer, which he calls a cousin of homeopathic proving and a harmonizing of inner narrative rather than a fix for a disease. Chance connects this to biofield tuning, where memories surface at specific points in the energy field, and argues that trauma work is about tracing how a personality adapted. Melissa agrees, saying habits people carry guilt about, from gym compulsion to an ADHD label, are adaptations rather than identity. Sympathy Versus Suppression, and the Search for the Simillimum Melissa distinguishes acting in sympathy with the body, as with saunas or fasting, from antipathic approaches she says can amount to green pharmacy. She contrasts classical homeopathy, which hunts the simillimum across the totality of a case, with the Narayani line, bottles labelled by disease name that combine several remedies, and with the fertility protocols she used in her first five years of practice. Kyle asks whether homeopathy has an equivalent of the doctrine of signatures, and Melissa points to the Prisma materia medica, the oyster shell behind Calcarea carbonica, and the match head image behind Phosphorus. Who Makes the Medicine, and the Resurgence Melissa says her former lecturer Peter, who first introduced her to homeopathy and now co teaches the academy, works on spagyric bases for remedies and has sourced material from Sajah Popham. Kyle describes living minutes from an anthroposophical medicine clinic near some of the first Rudolf Steiner farms, where makers emphasise an upward vortex when succussing, unlike Hahnemann banging the vial on his Bible. Both stress the maker's intention and state of mind. Melissa reports 570 sign ups to the academy's first cohort, against a usual 30 students a year, and a homeopathic hospital being built in Australia.

Alberta agrees the pattern is real, but doubts Fomenko's conclusion that true history is short and centered in Russia. The Almagest and the Wrong Sky The Almagest, the star catalog attributed to Ptolemy and dated to roughly 150 AD, is the cornerstone Fomenko tries to pull out. Because the vernal equinox drifts about one degree every 72 years, the ecliptic positions Ptolemy lists can be tested against computed skies, and Fomenko argues they match observations from somewhere between the 11th and 16th centuries rather than the second. Chance frames the stakes plainly: if a text this foundational can be checked by anyone with the Stellarium app and a translation of the alleged ancient Greek, the chronology stacked on top of it is under suspicion. At two or three years old, in the main quadrangle of Christ Church, Oxford, where his father lectured, he leaned too far over the fountain pool to watch the goldfish and fell in beneath the statue of Mercury, or Hermes, and his father hauled him out. He was never baptized as an infant, since both parents came from a nonconformist background, and when the usual age arrived he declined. Paganism, he notes, carries no doctrine of original sin to wash off, though it keeps rites of passage he believes the modern world has lost. A Man of the Circle, Not the Straight Line A rabbi's lecture McIntosh attended while living in New York gave him his sharpest distinction: in monotheism history runs in a straight line toward the second coming or the last judgment, while in polytheism everything moves in a great circle. He argues that this linear habit has migrated from religion into secular life, telling architects and artists never to look back, privileging the present over the past and eroding local cultural memory until only a global monoculture is left. His first book, written in his early twenties, was a history of astrology. Research before the internet meant rare volumes hunted at the British Library, the Watkins bookshop and the Atlantis shop in London, and trips abroad for manuscripts. A professor in Innsbruck sent him to a Masonic library in The Hague, whose Kloss collection held correspondence crucial to the thesis published as The Rose Cross and the Age of Reason. He has laid a circle of flat rune stones in his garden dedicated to the Norns, where shifting sunlight, a fallen leaf or a passing insect turns the circle into an oracle, and he practices stav, a Norwegian system of runic postures, daily. Skuld, the future Norn, is shown half veiled, which he reads as wyrd, a pattern that influences a life without wholly determining it. Sonja Testerman Are you being entrained by the music, or are you playing with the music? Are you a background instrument, or are you a lead virtuoso? You get to choose. Chance Garton Mind First, Matter Second Within minutes the two find common ground: reality begins in thought and only later hardens into matter. Sonja Testerman describes people as bundles of frequency that thicken into density, arguing that everything traces back to what she calls God sourced thought. Chance Garton flips the usual framing, insisting the body sits inside the mind rather than the mind inside the body, and offers that as the deepest explanation for why frequency based healing works at all. Testerman adds that physicality is roughly ten percent of reality, an afterthought pushed through from the unseen, with each frame of it built as we go. A Friendly Disagreement About Chakras Testerman presents the chakra system as a lockdown grid, claiming the top centers are coming off first so the whole brain can come online, and she ties this to an ongoing physical ascension in which organs relocate and glands enlarge. Garton pushes back gently. In his biofield tuning practice the energy centers are not a cage but an intellectual scaffolding for understanding how energy behaves, even if for many people they do function as limiters. He argues for languaging all of it in terms of empowerment rather than victimhood, so that newcomers on a Kundalini path are not handed fresh paranoia. Inside a Biofield Tuning Session Garton walks through the mechanics: an energy field roughly six feet in radius that he treats as mind and memory, read like the rings of a tree, where distance from the body maps to age. Working by phone, with crystals and candles standing in for the client's body on a table, he sweeps a tuning fork and listens for dissonance, noting its height, left or right, front or back. He describes tracing one client's pattern of frustration back to a C section birth, and another whose lifelong picky eating dissolved after a session touching father conditioning, followed by weight loss and new food cravings. Symptoms, Parasites and a Business Model The conversation turns sharply against mainstream medicine. Testerman argues there is no such thing as flu, that symptoms are the body detoxing and should be embraced, and that doctors a century and a half ago focused mainly on parasite control until, she claims, powerful banking families removed it and cancer appeared. She lists garlic, oregano oil, clove and cinnamon as everyday parasite fighters. Garton raises pleomorphism, the notion that bacteria shift form according to what the body needs cleaned up, and notes that germ means seed while biotic means life. These are contested claims well outside accepted medical science, presented as the speakers' own view. Sky as Playbook, Sky as Reflection Both reject standard cosmology, though they part ways on what the sky actually is. Testerman says the star map has not shifted in eight thousand years and points to sextant navigation and trigonometry as proof of a flat, domed reality, then recounts a remote viewing session in which Venus appeared as a self replicating crystal geode beaming to the North Star, together forming a nine dimensional projector broadcasting a playbook of events. Garton prefers reflection to projection, describing one life expressing itself as a melody with infinite instruments, and suggests deep alignment with imagination lets you play the score rather than be entrained by it.

Brandon Sterling From News Arrows to the Smart Money World Sterling traces his interest back to watching the up and down arrows on the news as a child, and to the 2008 crisis, which hit his father's work in the trades. The film The Big Short, about Michael Burry, showed him that traders could make money on markets going down as well as up. He says he began taking it seriously in 2019 after noticing hundreds of CEOs resign that fall, which he read as the sign of a coming black swan, then learned from mentors who had worked at pension funds, investment banks and hedge funds before trading his own capital. Saturn, Mercury and the Alchemy of Time Garton builds the episode's central image from a medieval alchemical engraving of Cronos, or Saturn, cutting Mercury off at the knees, and from Tracey Twyman's book Money Grows on the Tree of Knowledge, which argues that money only appears to be created ex nihilo and is really drawn from something intangible, time and human labor measured over time. Sterling supplies the modern figure on his slide: at a US average wage near thirty dollars an hour it now takes roughly 187 hours of work to buy one share of the S&P 500, against ten to twenty hours fifty years ago. Money Velocity and the Speeding Up of Life Sterling's slides argue that a thirty year mortgage has buyers paying for more than two houses once interest is counted, and that a 401k or IRA leaves a person long only and exposed to events like the 2020 crash. Garton reads Twyman on fractional reserve lending and money velocity, where a recession is a lack of velocity rather than simply a lack of money, and where inflating the supply while wages stay pegged to time means working longer for the same value as youth drains away. Garton calls the constant recession talk part of the spell. Pump and Dumps and the Trader as Sacrifice Sterling calls himself probably the world's biggest hater of crypto, describing Bitcoin as pure speculation with nothing backing it and the wave of celebrity coins as pump and dumps in the mold of Beanie Babies. He argues day trading works the same way, with online gurus telling followers to copy their trades and using them as liquidity to get out, and citing a Berkeley study he says ninety percent of day traders lose ninety percent of their money within ninety days. Garton reads Twyman on mortgage as death pledge and bond as bondage, calling the churn a sacrificial machine. Temple Coins, Put Options and Chosen Sacrifice Garton traces hedging back to Juno Moneta, the Roman goddess of memory and warning whose temple housed the mint, arguing that every coin was a receipt for a sacrifice and a hedge against divine wrath, and that where the ancients offered goats, wheat and incense, the modern trader offers a put option. Sterling defines a hedge as a trade made to reduce the risk of an adverse price move, answers Garton's ethics question by calling trading amoral because money and the corporate charter are artificial, and says he uses panicked headlines as liquidity to exit his positions.

Steve Falconer The Final Experiment Under the Microscope Chance Garton opens with the wave of headlines announcing that flat-earthers had reverted to the globe, and Steve Falconer argues the Antarctic trip was never an experiment at all: no control, no certainty about where the group actually stood, and no proof the light they filmed was the sun. He notes that Austin, the other flat-earth traveler, did not change his position and is almost never mentioned in the coverage. Falconer says he has since read Antarctic expedition journals from the late 1500s to the mid 1900s and found no mention of a 24-hour sun, only night, dusk and next morning. One Fact Cannot Cancel Another Chance reads a passage from the old Zetetic Astronomy book that Falconer had used in his first film, arguing that one fact can never contradict another and that both must be true. Falconer builds his answer around it, contending that a light in the sky over Antarctica cannot erase the lock and canal engineering he cites through New York State, Rochester and the Suez Canal, where he argues a roughly 630 foot cascade of curvature would be required and is absent. He also points to English law books that he says instruct engineers to assume a flat datum line and a plumb line. Why Falconer Thinks the Model Is Guarded Asked whether Antarctica functions as an inverted tower of Babel, with nations gathering at the periphery to obscure rather than seek the truth, Falconer contends the stakes are physics, religion and money at once. He argues everything is a toroidal field and that light is a perturbation in the ether, so a sealed perimeter would take Newtonian particle physics down with it. He contends that the Vatican's Unam Sanctam bull and the Gregorian calendar underwrite a copyright over name, date and place, comparing the all caps straw man to performing as Harry Potter and owing the author. He points listeners to Stephen Young's Fool's Wisdom. Day Lengths, Latitude Rings and Sun Trackers In the middle stretch Falconer describes auditing sunrise, sunset and day length figures for Antarctic stations across Wikipedia, Google Earth, Stellarium and time and date sites. He says three or four sources can disagree about the very same base, differing on when its 24-hour sun begins by anywhere from two days to about twenty-five, with one outlier he threw out after tracing it to two stations with similar names. He argues that matching latitudes north and south should share day lengths and do not. Chance adds that clock time and time zones impose uniformity while dividing people from one another. Mapping the Bases and the Old Expeditions For the final stretch Falconer previews part three of Scamtarctica, made with a mapmaker named Rob and his returning Spacebusters partner Ross, plotting stations and expedition tracks onto Alex Gleason's flat map. He raises the SANAE IV knife story, where a crew was reported stranded for 190 days although Troll Station and other bases sit within a couple hundred miles on the globe, and argues those gaps widen along an ice wall perimeter. He questions the South Pole base location against Scott's journal coordinates, notes that the round-Antarctica yacht race stops at Cape Town, India and Australia, and blames phone magnets for the trip's compass trouble.

James Frosch Spent Mushroom Blocks Become Garden Soil Frosch describes Family Fungi as a mushroom farm whose most valuable output is not the mushrooms but the spent mycelium blocks left after one or two flushes, which stop being commercially viable once they take up shelf space. He drives 25 to 30 minutes to a local sawmill, takes the hardwood waste stream from lumber headed into people's houses, grows it out, then returns it to the ground. In South Louisiana, with its very high water table and heavy clay, he says the blocks need about eight months to break down into something he compares to rich Dutch chocolate cake, and stacked in thirties they keep fruiting in the garden. Quantity Farming Versus Qualitative Nourishment Garton argues that people treat food like putting gas in a car, judging only whether the tank is full, while Frosch calls boxed products food stuff: made from food, but no longer food. Frosch says he takes issue with organic labeling loopholes, observes that hurricane shelves empty first of pop tarts and beer, and estimates his family produces roughly 20 percent of its calories from about a quarter acre of intensive perennial and mixed annual planting on their four acres. Garton frames industrialization as a genuine answer to an old problem, feeding everyone, that has now produced a new one worth tackling. Where A Beginner Should Start With Fungi Asked what a novice should cultivate, Frosch names oyster mushrooms first: easy at home from a grow kit or from spawn on hardwood sawdust, expandable into fresh wood chips or freshly cut logs, widely available and forgiving of neglect. He puts reishi second, grown on a countertop, harvested fresh and dehydrated for tea, or extracted in neutral spirits such as vodka or brandy, with the 190 proof organic alcohol his farm uses as one option and a charcoal filter recommended for vodka. Third is king stropharia, the wine cap or garden giant, which he says will only fruit with soil organisms and a casing layer. Soil As A Living Sub Aquatic System Frosch separates saprotrophic fungi that break down hardwood from mycorrhizal fungi that partner with tree roots, calling the latter the unsung heroes of the food chain for extending root systems enormously and mining minerals with acids like oxalic acid that plants cannot produce. He cites a line he heard from Matt Powers and John Kempf that soil is a sub aquatic system, roughly 20,000 gallons of water per acre in the first foot. He also reports that oyster mushrooms can remediate nematodes, which cause the root knot that once cost him a whole sweet potato harvest. Weeds, Books And Permission To Start Frosch's land was a strawberry plantation 60 to 70 years ago and pine forest savanna before that, and he says it was strip mined for minerals, so he now reads weeds like thistle as indicators of deficiency, uses no herbicides, and mulches or does a chop and drop instead. For study he points to the Louisiana Herb Journal, Matt Powers on regenerative soil, John Kempf on bio fertilizers, and Masanobu Fukuoka's One Straw Revolution and The Natural Way of Farming. He describes the great mother tea his wife Elise first blended for herself, warns against expert-itis, and says a few pots on a balcony is enough to begin.

Esotericism and the Useful Lies of the Ancients Chance lays out a long case that ancient priests and philosophers hid their real doctrines on purpose, for defense against charges of heresy or atheism, and for social stability. He cites the noble lie of Plato's Republic and the Athenian doctrine of autochthony, the claim that ancestors sprang from the soil with the tools of their caste already in hand, as a story that justified conquest and kept the lower castes in place. He collects mottoes from Ovid, from Epicurus, and from Bishop Synesius of Cyrene, who advised loving wisdom at home and embracing fables abroad, alongside Proverbs 25:2. Charles Blount, Robert Taylor, and the Lord Who Is Not God Chance reads at length from Charles Blount's 1680 Great Is Diana of the Ephesians, on how princes governed an unruly creature through hope and fear, raising in the conscience what Blount calls a whip of torture, the fear of future punishment. Dylan then turns to Robert Taylor's Astronomico-Theological Lectures, written in prison, and to Taylor's warning never to confound the Lord with God. Taylor treats them as particular and general terms, reading Judges 11:24 and Jephthah's bargain with the children of Ammon as evidence that each nation claimed its own tutelary planet rather than a universal deity. Yova, Adonai and the Sun That Hides in Winter The thumbnail quote is Psalm 89:46, which Dylan renders not as Lord but as Jove or Yova, how long will you hide. He derives the name from hava, to fall or to become, the same letters read elsewhere as Eve and as life, separated only by context. Chance walks through the Adonis myth, Myrrha turned into the myrrh tree, the buried seed, the fostering by Persephone, and a death and resurrection. Dylan counters that the horns may track local herding instead, and offers the Italian malocchio, bull horns hung over shops to ward off evil, as the root of the rock and roll hand sign. extra.jacob-diaz-undercover-virologist: Welcome and Dr. Jacob Diaz Returns to InnerVerse From Almost Becoming a Cop to Terrain Practitioner Self Teaching Outside the Medical School Paradigm Symptoms Are Messages from the Body The Caduceus and the Old Priesthood of Healers Why the Mainstream Compartmentalizes the Body The Elevator Pitch Against Germ Theory Strep Throat Decoded Through the Terrain Model The Noble Lie and Why Germs Replaced Demons Why People Get Better After Antibiotics Robert Koch, Tuberculin, and the German Connection Penicillin Comes From a Germ The Long Term Damage of Antibiotic Use Sepsis and the 60% False Positive Rate Isopathics as the Inverse of Antibiotics Three Client Success Stories: Pneumonia, Eczema, Shingles Why Holistic Practitioners Stay Curious Raising a Healthy Baby in the Terrain Model It's a one-way street when converting out of the belief that invisible boogeymen are making you sick and there's nothing about your own behaviors that could stop it. Chance Garton From Aspiring Cop to Undercover Virologist Diaz tells Chance Garton that before the lockdown years he was a typical American diet follower headed into law enforcement, and that he stepped away after asking whether he could enforce mandates that clashed with the Christian principles he was raised on. He describes finding Alec Zeck, Amanda Vollmer and Mike Winner and the End of COVID archive he first discussed on InnerVerse episode 94, then five plus years of self-schooling through the Baileys, Kaufman, Cowan and Mike Stone, mentorship under a naturopathic doctor he names as Mary Arch, a naturopathic practitioner certification, the Bigelson academy for blood work, and finally his own practice at terrainuv.com. Terrain Is Not a Theory, Diaz Argues Diaz objects to the phrase terrain theory at all, arguing that terrain simply names everything a person eats, thinks, feels and lives inside, and he contends that symptoms are the body communicating rather than the disease itself. He quotes Harvey Bigelson's line that health is simple and people are complicated. Garton, who works as a biofield tuner, adds the caduceus and the Therapeutae trained at ancient Alexandria as signs that germs now occupy the slot older systems gave demons, and both argue that a medicine split into cardiac, neurological and back specialists mirrors a compartmentalized body rather than a whole one. The Elevator Pitch Against Germ Theory Asked how he opens with a skeptic, Diaz says he asks people how many germs they carry, then claims the body holds roughly ten to a hundred times more germs than blood cells. He points to streptococcus living in every throat and asks why nobody has strep throat daily, likens the gut to soil microbiology that any farmer would recognize, and argues the classical contagion proofs depended on injecting unpurified cultures into the abdomens of guinea pigs rather than on natural exposure. Germs, he contends, are saprophytes eating dead and dying tissue, the pleomorphic microzymes described by Bechamp, Naessens and Enderlein. Koch, Tuberculin and the Antibiotic Question Garton asks why people seem to get better after antibiotics. Diaz calls that reasoning the fallacy of affirming the consequent, then recounts his reading of the history: Robert Koch experimenting with petrochemical dyes, the tuberculin failure that Diaz says killed thousands and got Koch pushed out of Germany, and Bismarck later paying him to blame British ships coming through the Suez Canal. Diaz notes that penicillin is a metabolite of a fungus rather than an anti-germ agent, and contrasts antibiotics with the isopathics Gunther Enderlein set out in Bacterial Cyclology. Garton frames germ fear as a modern version of Plato's noble lie. Sepsis Statistics and the Cases He Recounts Late in the hour Diaz cites roughly 1.7 million United States sepsis cases a year, a twenty to sixty percent false positive range in the literature, and a forty percent false positive rate for the blood cultures called the gold standard, alongside studies from the 1800s and 1900s that he says induced sepsis in animals with no bacteria present. He recounts three client stories as claims about his own practice: a young girl whose pneumonia he says cleared quickly, a woman told she had shingles, and a client with Bell's palsy beside a hearing implant. He closes calling microzymes the chi or prana of the body.

Virtue as Vir, Marketers as Magi, and a Dream About Forgetting Virtue, Pantano says, is not decorum but vir, the Indo-European root for hero, one step above humanity and one below the gods, reached by purgation and the seven virtues tied to the seven illuminating lights. Camille Sauvé Three Ages of Stone Stacked on Top of Each Other Camille Sauvé builds much of her book Sorcerers of Stone on the work of a Cuscanian researcher named Alfredo Gamara, who identified three distinct construction styles in Peru and called them Hananpacha, Uranpacha and Ukupacha. Her central visual argument is over building: an older style sits underneath the megalithic work, and the far more recent Inca, Kilke and Ware masonry sits on top of and around both, often fitted into the grooves and recesses of the oldest layer. Sauvé argues that later cultures recognized this earlier work as sacred and deliberately built into it rather than replacing it. The Hananpacha Layer Nobody Talks About Sauvé says the megalithic walls get all the attention while the stranger, older Hananpacha work goes largely unstudied. These are gray metamorphosed limestone forms that read as art projects rather than buildings: stepped chicanas, carved basins, surreal shapes with no windows, doorways or ceilings and no obvious use as shelter. She reports finding the same forms far outside Peru, in Japan, Bulgaria, Germany, beneath the Egyptian pyramids, and in the foundation stone under the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, where both Jewish and Muslim tradition place the creation of the earth. That global spread, she contends, points toward a single worldwide civilization. Seke Lines, Charged Rock and Doorways to Elsewhere Sauvé describes 42 seke lines radiating out from the Coricancha sun temple in Cusco, with the huacas, or sacred sites, placed directly along them. She suggests these lines follow fracture zones and underground water passages, creating discontinuity zones where telluric currents flow and where quartz rich rock can hold electromagnetic charge. Andean pacos and shamans still come to these places to pray to the Apus and Pachamama and, she believes, to enter altered states. The Bullying Pattern He Kept Recreating He describes hiding in the library until dark to avoid bullies, then watching the same dynamic follow him into high school as status and class, into engineering school where professors told him he should be an actor, and into jobs, friendships, and relationships he fled by moving hundreds or thousands of miles. The faces and personalities changed, he says, but the energy was identical, until he reached the realization that the only common element in every situation was himself. Clearing that pattern, he reports, brought nurturing and supportive people he had no prior concept of. Four Phases Of Programming, From Conception Onward Chari lays out a model with four phases: conception, where he says a percentage of each parent's and each grandparent's unresolved emotions transfers into the forming child; nine months in the womb, absorbing the mother's arguments and frustrations; birth and the direct interface with parents; and finally the years to thirteen or fourteen, when whatever is said goes in without evaluation. Garton adds his biofield tuning experience of reading cesarean births and guilt patterns off the energy field, and pushes back with a soul choice caveat so expectant parents do not carry extra fear. Missing Notes, Squashed Emotions, And Sympathetic Resonance Rather than working from what a client tells him, Chari says he listens to the sound spectrum of the voice itself, hunting for the deficient note among the twelve that repeat across a piano's hundreds of keys. A note he can barely hear or cannot hear at all signals, in his account, an emotion squashing that key: anger, grief, self sabotage, worry, low self worth. His fix borrows sympathetic resonance, the way striking A on one piano vibrates the same string on an untouched second piano, to bring the missing note back up. Humming Your Way Back Into Tune The baseline program, Chari explains, is homework by email: music written in the key of the note that went quiet, roughly ten minutes of humming or singing along with a free phone tuner app confirming the pitch, then twenty minute tracks playing in the background. The tuner is the feedback half of biofeedback. He reports personality shifts, clients finally being heard at work, and follow up sessions a week or two later where the note has returned. Maintenance runs about monthly, he says, comparing it to oil changes and belt levels rather than a one time fix.

Brandy Anderson From Depression to a Two Word Answer Anderson traces her turn inward to 2014, when a heaviness she had never known settled in and refused to lift, something she now reads as existential rather than clinical. One morning she prayed provocatively rather than piously, venting frustration into the air, and reports hearing a voice say be still, followed by a peace she could not explain. Lacking a framework, she plugged back into churches, studied theologies and scripture for years, found mainstream answers thin, and drifted toward contemplative and mystical Christianity alongside Buddhist and Hindu reading. A Grandmother Who Types on the Television The book's origin story is a family one. Anderson describes a grandmother who feared dying, resisted the crossing, and in doing so left what she calls an open portal. Months later the Roku search bar filled with the word hello, then love, and relatives fled the house screaming while an aunt eventually moved out. Anderson assumed a hacker until, she says, the responses began answering questions before anyone spoke them. Three years on she reports sustained contact through televisions, laptops, thermal printers and phone calls that show a disconnected landline on the caller ID. Energy as the Currency of the Other Side Much of the practical detail here is about cost. Anderson describes spirits needing energy to touch anything physical, which is why the early messages were single words and why the word help kept appearing. Fire, she says, restores that energy, so the family builds fires on request. The same logic explains the darker cases: a spirit spending its reserves to bite, scratch or throw things is running on hate. Chance Garton connects this to his own biofield tuning practice, where candles have always sat on the table on pure intuition. Anderson describes the crossing as a moment when full clarity falls on everything a person thought or did, not as a courtroom but as exposure, which is painful in proportion to how polished the mask was. Sin, in her reading, is less the bad things we do than being out of alignment inside; the behavior is only fruit. Garton adds that sin needs no punishment because it is its own, and later unpacks the linguistic case that hell names a valley and repentance means going beyond the mind. The Shadow, the Obstacle, and the Gold Anderson's Jungian coaching inverts the usual coaching bargain. Rather than vision boards and goal lists, she works into the obstacle itself, asking what it is rooted in, on the view that shadow material is unconscious rather than bad and never runs out. Garton agrees that dodging hurdles gets you disqualified, and argues the things we most avoid mark the direction we actually want. Anderson closes on the point that deepest fear and deepest desire share an address, that the gold sits in the shadow, and that the work is integration without judgment.

Chance Garton The Mountain That Might Be a Pachyderm The centerpiece of the conversation is Spain's Montgo massif, which Stellium7 argues may be the petrified remains of a colossal pachyderm rather than ordinary rock. He notes the formation reads as an elephant lying on its side from multiple angles, that a local restaurant once used it as a logo, and that a cave sits precisely where an eye socket belongs. He says he hiked it for eight years without the thought ever occurring to him, then found roughly ten anatomical features in a single hour on Google Earth once he entertained the possibility. Biology Underneath the Geology Textbook Stellium7 contends that even the mainstream account concedes most rock was once alive, with igneous stone the exception, and that sedimentary and metamorphic layers are compressed plant and animal remains. His departure is timescale: he argues petrification can happen fast rather than across hundreds of millions of years. He points to Lake Natron, whose alkaline water hardens creatures that fall in, to Mother Shipton's Cave in the UK where hung objects turn stony within months, and to Mount St. Helens, where he says layering and micro layering formed in a matter of hours. Gravity, Pressure and the Case for Giants The textbook objection to titanic creatures is weight: double a sphere's diameter and volume grows eightfold, so giants would break their own bones. Stellium7 counters that the objection depends entirely on gravity being what we are told, and he favors density, buoyancy and electrostatics as the operative forces. He notes the mainstream itself grants gigantism, citing meter long dragonflies, and asks how big the bears and elephants were. Chance adds that air may simply be a lighter density of water, and Stellium7 describes a pressurized room producing tens of thousands of oversized cherry tomatoes. He notes lava tubes resembling root structures, and both men trace the branching Lichtenberg or dendritic pattern through lightning, rivers, blood vessels and the fascial network. To guard against it he drew up a list of features he expected in an eye socket beforehand, consulted anatomy books, video of an elephant skeleton and 3D rendering software, noting seven bones form the orbit across mammals. He says critics invoked Dunning Kruger without reviewing his work, prompting a three hour rebuttal that took six weeks. Both are dialogues, staged conversations in which Socrates trades speeches with Timaeus, Critias and a fourth man, Hermocrates, who almost never gets mentioned. Critias says he heard the tale as a boy from his grandfather, who had it from his father, who had it from Solon around 600 BC. Kelley flags the oddest detail: about twenty modern pages into the Critias the text simply stops mid sentence, with no note and no explanation. The Methodology of Mythology The documentary follows George Sarantides, a Greek engineer and Platonic scholar whose paper on the methodology of mythology asks what Plato's myths were for. Kelley summarizes the position this way: the myths are not all true, since Zeus was not literally doing things on a Thursday, and not all false either, because real history and real observations about human nature sit inside them. If a story is neither, the responsibility shifts onto the reader to work out which parts are which. That, Kelley argues, is why Plato buried exact geometry and geography in the tale, above a door reading let no one ignorant of geometry enter here. Pelagos Is Not the Ocean The core linguistic claim is that Plato never calls the water around Atlantis Okeanos, the open ocean, a word he uses freely in other books. He writes Atlantic Pelagos, which Chance Garton describes as an inland or enclosed water, closer to the Aegean or the Adriatic. Kelley contends that translators who had never met the phrase simply assumed it meant the Atlantic Ocean, and that Victorian writers such as Ignatius Donnelly built the whole mid ocean continent on that guess. On this reading, the search for a sunken landmass out past Gibraltar was never indicated by the original text at all. Boundary Markers, Not Landmarks The second half of the location argument concerns the pillars of Heracles. Kelley notes that ancient authors could not agree on what they even were, calling them mountains, islands or actual columns, and placed them variously at the strait between Sicily and Italy, at the passage from the Aegean to the Black Sea, and, in Tacitus, as far north as the mouth of the Rhine. Sarantides went back to Plato's original ancient Greek, where the word also means a stela, a commemorative marker. The documentary contends the Greeks planted such markers at the edge of exploration, so the pillars moved outward as their seafaring did. Northwest Africa and the Green Sahara The film's punchline, as Kelley puts it, is that the lands described seem to match northwestern Africa during the early Holocene green Sahara, an uncontroversial climate period when mega lakes stood where desert is now, taking in Mauritania and the Richat structure the film investigates as a possible Atlantean remnant. Garton adds that the Atlas mountains sitting right there would explain the name. Kelley is careful that this rests on Plato's exact wording plus modern climate science, and he reads the deeper story as philosophy: Athena backing Athens, Poseidon backing Atlantis, and a divine bloodline diluting into greed.

Serena describes the division of labor with affection: Kyle is the Aquarius, the creative, the wizard, the druid who makes concoctions, while she is the Sagittarius who says let's make it real and gets a label on the bottle. Before they combined forces she was living in Italy and he was in Wisconsin. Their son Davide arrived after the shop, which they call their first born. Fertility As A Conversation For Two Serena opens the fertility discussion by pushing back on the assumption that conception is the woman's problem alone, saying it takes two and that the responsibility of creation should be shared. Kyle describes what he sees at the shop counter, where a woman approaches with a question while her partner waits on what they affectionately call the boyfriend couch, a little chair off in the corner. Kyle says the practice he likes to preserve is having that conversation with both partners present, and he contends that the man's own state of health is part of the picture, a turn in the conversation the boyfriend rarely expects. Doctrine Of Signatures And Plant Lore A large share of the episode is Kyle's interpretive method rather than any protocol. He reads plants through what he calls his astro herbal chart, assigning them to Venus, Mars, the Moon or Virgo, and pairing every Venusian softness with a Martian counterpart, because where there is a princess there is always a prince, the thorn and the bramble. He layers in the alchemical triad of salt, sulfur and mercury and the principles of three. He also detours into folklore, noting that Achillea takes its name from Achilles, taught by the centaur Chiron, and calling the old leaves of three warning a psyop against learning to identify poison ivy. Grief, Identity And The Passage To Motherhood The most personal stretch is Serena on what changes in a woman after loss or after birth. She frames the postpartum shift as a question of identity: you once were a maiden, now you are a mother, so you have lost what you were before, grieving a self you knew while meeting a newer self you do not know yet, becoming a stranger to yourself. The heartbeat, she says, is the rhythm of the present moment, an answer to a mind stuck in what if. In the outro Chance and his wife Jennifer speak about their own loss the previous year and how many women quietly wrote to her afterward. The Father To Be, Flower Essences And Whole Plants Chance asks what supports the man taking on the mantle of fatherhood, and Kyle answers with categories rather than prescriptions. He defines adaptogens as plants said to help every system adapt to stress, then spends time on Wisconsin's American ginseng industry near Wausau, which he describes as heavily pesticided and expensive, arguing for a trusted organic grower. He praises a flower essence called Truth Teller, labeled conviction, and describes what a man running a business pushes down instead of saying. Kyle also makes a craft case against essential oils, noting it takes forty roses to make a single drop, preferring whole plants in carrier oils.

extra.robert-falconer-ifs: Welcome & Intro: The Mind, the Biofield and the Many Within Robert's Path: From Severe Trauma to Healing Practitioner Plato, the Daoists and Ancient Multiple-Parts Models of Mind The Internal Civil War: Why Most People Burn Up Energy Fighting Themselves Self With a Capital S: The Witness That Cannot Be Damaged Richard Schwartz and the Birth of Internal Family Systems The Cutting Patient: How IFS Discovered Respect for Every Part Managers, Firefighters and Exiles: The Three Categories of Parts Talking to Your Parts: How a Session Actually Works Legacy Burdens and the Diaz Wrestler Experiment in Epigenetics Unattached Burdens: When Something Inside Isn't a Part of You Spirit Possession as a Universal Human Phenomenon The Bloodshot Eyeball: Bob's Case That Opened the Door Does our mind itself have a similar menagerie of coexistent components merging into and out of the psychic spotlight as needed? Robert Falconer Bob Falconer's Road to Parts Work Falconer opens by saying he came to this work because he desperately needed healing himself, after a childhood he describes as extremely abusive. He worked through most of the therapies on offer and found that the ones that helped were all parts based: Gestalt at the Esalen Institute, the Watkins ego state therapy, voice dialogue, psychosynthesis and Pia Mellody's post induction therapy. About twenty years ago he found Internal Family Systems, which he calls the most potent and the most respectful of them. He also argues the idea is ancient, pointing to a Socratic dialogue where inner debate is treated as obvious proof that a mind is made of parts. How Richard Schwartz Stumbled Into IFS Falconer credits Richard Schwartz, whom everyone calls Dick, with discovering rather than inventing IFS about forty years ago. Schwartz was a tenured family therapy professor testing whether reorganizing families would resolve their children's eating disorders, and as Falconer retells it, the children did not realize they had been cured and kept doing the behaviors. So Schwartz started asking what was going on inside them instead. The turning point Falconer describes came when Schwartz tried to team up with one client's other parts to argue a protective part out of its job, watched that backfire badly, and instead began a respectful conversation with the protector. Protectors, Exiles, Managers and Firefighters The model Falconer lays out has two basic kinds of parts. Protectors work to stop or prevent emotional pain, and exiles, usually much younger, are the ones carrying it. Protectors divide again into managers, which are proactive and socially acceptable, such as the workaholic, the perfectionist and the inner critic, and firefighters, which arrive once the manager's strategy stops working and which, he says, do not care about collateral damage. Order matters in his account: practitioners go to the protectors first for permission before witnessing and unburdening the exiles. Experience varies, with roughly eighty percent seeing images, Schwartz hearing voices instead, and others reporting Eugene Gendlin's felt sense. Legacy Burdens and the Startled Rats Past a person's own history, Falconer says, come legacy burdens, material that is not from the individual's lifetime at all. He points to Rachel Yehuda, who he says has published more than 500 peer reviewed papers on neurochemical changes in the children and grandchildren of Holocaust survivors, and to an experiment run by Dias in Atlanta with a Harvard collaborator named Ressler. Male rats were conditioned with a shock until an almond like smell alone triggered a startle response, their sperm was used to impregnate females that had never met them, and the pups startled at the same smell. Falconer calls the epigenetics behind this hard science. Unattached Burdens and the Case That Changed Him Deeper still, Falconer argues, sit what IFS calls unattached burdens, presences he says belong neither to the person nor to their ancestors, and which he is willing to describe using the older cross cultural language of spirit possession. He recounts a training session where a woman's savage inner critic offered none of the good intention a genuine part would, and answered plainly when asked whether it was part of her. Staff nicknamed him Bob the Ghostbuster, and a later email from that woman redirected his career into the decade of research behind The Others Within Us. Chance closes by cautioning listeners against reaching for possession as a first explanation.

Being Called Crazy for Fifty Years The thread running through Ray's account with Chance Garton is rejection. As a boy hiding in basements and closets for hours, he saw energy in walls and talked with beings he thought everyone could see, and was told never to say it again. Paramedics who heard him ask about the voice and the light decided he was not all right. His mother said it never happened. A maintenance man who checked his haunted apartment a hundred times told him to stop calling. Ray explains how that verdict pushed him into insomnia, drinking, drugs and eventually rehab. The Father in Law on the Movie Screen After his future wife bought him a distance clearing for his birthday, Ray started seeing a heavy, bearded, dark haired man on what he calls the movie screen in his third eye, repeating that he had made a mistake and that Ray could help her. His wife, a doctor of psychology and neuropsychology, recognized the description as her dead father and showed a later photo that matched. Instead of diagnosing him, she suggested he was a psychic medium. Ray tells Chance the message he carried actually saved someone's life, and that once delivered, the man stopped appearing. Mentors, Turning It On and Turning It Off The medium Ray finally sat with described the vibrations, lines, swirls and screen exactly as he saw them, told him she had been institutionalized for schizophrenia as a girl, and took him on as a mentee. Her core teaching was control. Ray explains to Chance that the dead only want a message delivered, so refusing plainly makes them leave, while setting an open window like tomorrow afternoon in the living room invites them in. A second mentor, the artist who drew his wife's father, chose eleven applicants from hundreds and became the father figure Ray never had. Thermodynamics, Dark Energy and the Buddha Ray likes attaching physics to spiritual claims. He leans on the first law of thermodynamics, that energy cannot be created or destroyed, to argue that consciousness emitted by the brain has to go somewhere at death. His candidate is dark energy, the roughly sixty nine percent of the universe nobody can locate, dark only because we cannot see it. On purpose he cites the Buddha saying on his deathbed that this was his seventh life and he would not return, meaning enlightenment ends the cycle and turns you into a guide for someone else.
extra.christopher-mcintosh-tetrad: Why Magic Gets a Bad Name How This Novel Came to Be The Crowley Disciple Who Inspired Gilbert North Science Religion Art and Magic The Magic Hidden Inside Mathematics Concerts and Plays as Secret Rituals Why Black Magic Is Like Black Electricity Hidden Forces Behind Political Movements Do You Believe in the Devil Look at Reality and Find the Miraculous Keeping a Magical Diary Saying Yes to the Universe Is magic something that we lose in puberty, only attainable through some doctor's strange pilgrimage to a far-off Carmetage? Or are there simple ways in which we can reframe our experiences that invoke something a little more synchronistic and sublime in ourselves? Chance Garton And so I create in a way a kind of egregore, an egregore being a thought form, a collective thought form on the invisible plane created by a group of people thinking the same thoughts and focusing on the same symbols and ideas. Christopher McIntosh what you're doing in magic is you are saying to yourself, I'm going to act as if the world that I'm working in were true. Christopher McIntosh the way that it works is because at the deepest level of ourselves we're connected to the whole universe and the universe is everything in the universe is connected by invisible fields and one sort of all-encompassing field this is what the French magician Elifaz Levy called the astral light Christopher McIntosh where Mephistopheles appears and Faust asks him who he is and he says I'm a part of that power which always wills the bad and always does the good or always causes the good and so he's in a way like the grain of sand in the oyster which is an irritant which in the end produces a pearl Christopher McIntosh which means that the real jester is the profound truth teller and who's skilled enough to do it in a way that can bring levity to what is otherwise a painful truth Chance Garton you say you believed yourself to witness miracles in fact what happened was that you looked for the miraculous and found reality now you must look at reality and find the miraculous Christopher McIntosh everyone even the purest scientist working in the utmost isolation has to decide in the depths of his being whether he is going to say yes or no to the universe or else postpone the decision which is another way of saying no at the moment it is the knows who rule the world Chance Garton A Novel Built From a Real Occult Apprenticeship Chance Garton and Christopher McIntosh open with the origin of Return of the Tetrad, the 2013 novel Mandrake of Oxford published after decades in a drawer. McIntosh sketches four phases of his own life, from Christian upbringing to rationalist skepticism to astrology, Rosicrucianism and a doctoral thesis on an eighteenth century neo-Rosicrucian order. The mentor figure Gilbert North is loosely based on Gerald Yorke, once Aleister Crowley's chief disciple, who amassed the Crowley archive he later donated to a London library. The narrator, journalist Paul Cairns, is largely McIntosh as a young man. Four Ways of Operating in the World The heart of the conversation is Lionel Snell, who writes as Ramsey Dukes, and his first book SSOTBME, which McIntosh says he personally prompted him to write. Snell maps four modalities, science, religion, art and magic, onto Carl Jung's four functions. Science is observation plus reason, religion reason plus intuition, art intuition plus feeling, and magic feeling plus observation. McIntosh argues that much of what we call science or art is really magic that nobody wants to name. He illustrates the as if principle with Snell's maths lesson on the square root of minus one. Rituals We Perform Without Noticing McIntosh reframes ordinary cultural life as ritual. Watching Hamlet is a magical act because the audience suspends disbelief and immerses itself as though the play were real. An orchestral concert is another, with the tension of tuning, the silence, the conductor raising a baton that functions as a magic wand. Garton extends this with the Cage piece he calls 433, where the same silent performance feels different each time because of coughs and the psychic energy of the room. Both agree that fiction writing creates egregores, collective thought forms that outlive their authors. Black Electricity and the Question of Evil Garton reads the novel's line that black magic is a term used by simpletons, and that talking about black magic is like talking about black electricity. McIntosh calls the saints of evil speech narrative theatrics, but agrees magic is a neutral force that rebounds on anyone who uses it for harm. He describes Eliphas Levi's astral light, borrowed later by the Theosophists, as the field where egregores live, some of them genuinely unpleasant. He points to Stephen Flowers and The Occult Roots of Bolshevism, plus the Ernest Butler and Dolores Ashcroft-Nowicki entity transfer story from Herbie Brennan's Whispers. Loki, the Cosmic Joke and Staying in the Wow Asked whether he believes in the devil as an individual, McIntosh says no, then turns to Loki and the line from Goethe's Faust where Mephistopheles calls himself part of the power that wills the bad and causes the good. Loki is the grain of sand that makes the pearl, and the jester whose mockery deflates authority, which is why dictatorships hate humor. extra.mark-gober: An End to Upside Down Thinking: Mark Gober's Consciousness Thesis From the Trading Floor to the Rabbit Hole: The First Domino CIA Declassified: Remote Viewing, Veridical NDEs, and Six-Sigma Psi Mystical Experiences and the Brain-as-Transducer Model Past Lives, Precognition, and Memory Beyond the Brain Spoon Bending, Psychic Kids, and the Skeptic Obstruction Machine The Dark Night Question: Evil, Suffering, and Compassion with Discernment Chance's Outro: Mediumship, Fraud, and Personal Reflection I was a hardcore materialist and increasingly so as I got older where I thought, well, just science shows us that those old superstitious spiritual religious beliefs, there's nothing to them.
