Mark Gober From Wall Street Materialist To Consciousness Author Gober opens by stressing how different he used to be: a Princeton graduate and tennis captain who became a New York investment banker through the 2008 financial crisis, then a partner at a Silicon Valley strategy firm, and by his own description a hardcore materialist who assumed science had emptied out the old spiritual claims. He dates the turn to the summer of 2016, when podcasts, books and papers became the first domino, and began writing a year later. Six books in the upside down series followed, plus the podcast Where Is My Mind and a board seat at the Institute of Noetic Sciences. The Evidence Gober Puts In Front Of Skeptics Asked what he finds most compelling, Gober gives three items. First, the CIA documents declassified from the remote viewing program the US government began in the 1970s, which he says state that remote viewing is a real phenomenon, that the implications are revolutionary and the evidence too impressive to dismiss as coincidence; he notes another document declassified days before this April 2024 conversation. Second, Dr. Jessica Utts, the 2016 president of the American Statistical Association, who wrote in a 1995 report that psychic functioning has been well established. Third, Dean Radin's Real Magic, whose sixth chapter reports six sigma results across telepathy, psychokinesis, remote viewing and precognition. Near Death Experiences And Verified Memories Gober argues the strongest near death cases are veridical out of body ones, where a patient in cardiac arrest reports what they saw or overheard and bystanders confirm it. He cites the book The Self Does Not Die, which collects about a hundred such accounts, Dr. Bruce Greyson of the University of Virginia, whose line that the mind functions better than ever when the brain is not functioning he calls a total reversal of the materialist paradigm, and Dr. Jan Holden of the University of North Texas, who told him these cases wipe out the physiological explanations. Kenneth Ring's Mindsight, on blind experiencers who report sight, extends the point. Time, Precognition And Rewriting The Story Of Your Past The conversation then turns to time. Gober revisits Daryl Bem's precognition studies covered by the New York Times, where subjects who studied only after taking a test did better on it, alongside experiments where the body responds before an image appears on screen. He says the definition of time is circular and the past is only an inference, and he borrows David Hawkins's picture of light through a prism producing a hologram viewed from different angles inside one ever present now. Garton answers with biofield tuning work, including reframing a client's Chinese medicine story about her mother's miscarriages and lost Jing, and Gober adds Byron Katie's four questions. Suppression, Spiritual War And Compassion With Discernment Closing the free hour, Gober describes organized resistance to this material: guerrilla skeptics rewriting Wikipedia pages, Rupert Sheldrake's entry branding him pseudoscientific, cofounder Larry Sanger calling the site propaganda, and neuroscientist Mario Beauregard telling the Skeptiko podcast that a Canadian institute head would never let him study the brain spiritually. Gober reads this as social engineering and, drawing on An End to Upside Down Contact, as a spiritual war of dark and light that he argues still serves evolution. Responding to a Rupert Spira passage that we are literally each other, he contends oneness alone is insufficient and calls for compassion with discernment.

Chance Garton The Law Of Octaves As A Cosmic Principle Robert Comber describes the organizing idea behind his forthcoming 400 plus page book, The Lost Octave, as what he calls the lore of octaves: on a piano the eighth note ends one octave and begins the next, so the beginning is the end and the end is the beginning. He argues this makes consciousness spherical rather than linear, and that recognizing it in advance lets a person relax into their journey instead of endlessly seeking. Comber ties it to the final two I Ching hexagrams, before completion and after completion, and to the dark night of the soul he says he passed through twice. Where Comber Says The I Ching Actually Started Comber traces the I Ching to a post cataclysm world roughly 8,000 years ago, well earlier than the conventional dating he acknowledges he is contradicting. He describes it beginning as bigrams, only eight possible combinations of two lines, used to read seasons, rains, wind and thunder. Royalty later turned it toward divination with yarrow sticks and then coins, and only around the King Wen period, four to five thousand years ago, did it become six line hexagrams, with Lao Tzu and Confucius layering philosophy on top. He also points to African priests casting shells and drawing lines in sand as a parallel binary code, citing physicist Dr James Gates. The Lion's Gate Map That Turned 64 Into 72 Comber says the whole system arrived on the 8/8 Lion's Gate while he was studying a human design year wheel and felt a gap in it. Using clock mathematics, since 60 seconds and 60 minutes govern a 360 degree circle, he placed hexagrams 1 through 60 around the rim and set 61 through 64 at the four cardinal directions in the center. He links that to the Hebrew sacred name of God, to Venus starting her synodic cycle in Leo, and to the eight pointed star of Ishtar and Inanna, doubled into a hypercube. Master Gates, A Seventh Line, And 432 Comber contends the original written first hexagram carried a seventh line, and that this seventh line is how the system moves into a fourth dimensional plane. He claims his eight new gates each landed on a different zodiac sign with no repeats, producing twelve master gates, one per sign, which he believes was once a verbal transmission passed master to student and then lost. He notes 64 hexagrams times six lines gives 384 archetypes, while 72 times six gives 432, the number he ties to harmonic tuning and the Giza measurements. He frames the shift as binary code moving into ternary code, and two strand DNA toward three strand. Star Lore, Correspondences, And Trusting Your Own Ear Comber prefers the term star lore, spelled l o r e, to astro theology, calling it the spoken story of the stars from which he says myths, fairy tales and Bible episodes derive. He reads the eclipse as the stone of the tomb, the moon that rolls away, noting three days is 72 hours. He points to the elements of earth, fire, water, air and ether, noting that Chinese thought substitutes metal and wood, and to the threefold divisions everywhere: the tridosha of Ayurveda, the three treasures and the dantian of Chinese medicine, the cardinal, fixed and mutable modes of astrology, and alchemy's three philosophical principles of sulfur, mercury and salt. From the Prima Materia through duality to the elements, he argues, the same archetypal pattern is macrocosmic and microcosmic, present in every person and every plant in differing ratios. Gnosis Cardiaca: Knowledge Through The Heart Garton reads a passage from the book on gnosis cardiaca, and Popham credits the idea largely to the late Stephen Harrod Buhner and his book The Secret Teachings of Plants, acknowledging that the science in it has come under scrutiny. The premise, as Popham relays it, is that everything emanates an electromagnetic frequency carrying information, and that the human heart is the body's greatest oscillator, able to entrain with other fields. He uses a radio dial as the analogy: you tune past static until the fields synchronize. He is candid that it is also easy to mistake your own thoughts for something received. Why He Calls It Evolutionary Herbalism Popham argues Western herbalism has lurched through identity crises while Chinese medicine, Ayurveda, Tibetan medicine, Kampo and Unani Tibb held continuity for centuries. His evolutionary model deliberately layers those stages rather than choosing between them: folk and bioregional practice where people learned from the plants themselves, the vitalist and energetic systems reading hot, cold, wet and dry, and the modern biomedical work on plant chemistry and double blind placebo controlled studies. Science has a lot to offer, he says, but he does not think we should abandon tradition for its sake. He names his contribution as reviving Western alchemy and medical astrology, once mainstream in the Renaissance. Treating The Person, Not The Disease Asked how his holistic evaluation works, Popham frames a symptom as a language, a communication that something deeper is off, and contrasts that with what he calls allopathic herbalism, the use this herb for that symptom mindset. He describes constitutional or tissue state assessment across three variables: temperature, moisture, and the tonal quality of the tissue. Beyond that he wants the whole timeline of a person's life, home, family and food, sometimes taking over two hours for an initial consultation, alongside tools like pulse and tongue reading, blood work and, for him, medical astrology. A teacher's line stuck with him: reaching first for an herb misses the point entirely. Poison Into Medicine As Inner Alchemy The conversation turns toward reframing. Popham holds that everyone carries trauma to varying degrees and that healing means refusing the role of constant victim, reorienting perception so the experience teaches something and turns weakness into strength. He connects this to what he calls the practical premise of laboratory alchemy, poison into medicine, applied inwardly. His final step in evaluation is to ask which archetypal forces, elemental or planetary, are excessive or deficient in a person, and how to turn that force from its dark side toward its light side. extra.sophie-fletcher-human-design: Meet Sophie Fletcher, PhD in depth psychology Raised in a spiritual community from age four Why the body and mind were never separate Ra Uru Hu channels the human design system The science of differentiation The five types and the sacral energizer bunny Projectors, auras, and waiting for the invitation Nobody is designed to decide with the mind Emotional authority and surfing your own wave The 400 year cycle switching in 2027 Biofield tuning and the residue left behind Channeled material and your own discernment I had really always been interested in people, like what makes people people, what makes you different than me, what makes certain people make certain choices. Chance Garton From spiritual community to a depth psychology PhD Sophie Fletcher tells Chance Garton she was raised inside a spiritual community from around age four, a framework she credits with keeping her grounded even as it fed a habit of dissociating into what she calls the dorsal, shut down side of the nervous system. She studied philosophy and psychoanalysis, finished a first master's in spiritual psychology at 24, then met a bodyworker trained in Chinese meridian theory whose wife used human design in her coaching. Human design and somatic work arrived together for her. She later completed a second master's and a PhD in depth psychology with a somatic emphasis at Pacifica Graduate Institute. The six sciences behind the human design system Fletcher reports that human design was transcribed by a man later known as Ra Uru Hu, who said a voice delivered the material to him. He taught it, then told his students to burn everything and disappeared, returning later to rebuild the system from notes the students had quietly kept. As she presents it, the system combines four esoteric sciences, a nine chakra Hindu model, the Kabbalistic tree of life, the I Ching and astrology, with two modern ones, the 64 DNA codons and neutrinos, which she describes as the smallest particles that carry mass and information. She works with tropical rather than sidereal charts. Five types, five auras, five ways of working The body graph, Fletcher explains, sorts people into five types. Generators and manifesting generators are the energy types at roughly 70 percent of the population, defined by a lit up sacral center she likens to an energizer bunny, with an enveloping aura and a strategy of responding rather than initiating. Manifestors are about 8 percent, the only type designed to initiate, carrying a fixed and repelling aura. Projectors, about 20 percent and her own type, have a penetrating aura and are meant to wait for recognition and invitation. Reflectors, about 1 percent, have no defined centers and a sampling aura she says is ruled by the moon. Authority is the body deciding, not the mind Fletcher calls authority the most practical piece of the system, each person's designed route to a decision, and says that in human design nobody at all is built to make a final call from the mind. A defined spleen, she describes, gives one quiet instinctual read that speaks only once. A defined sacral answers in the now through sounds and physical movement, and she has clients practice on low stakes choices like pointing at things in the refrigerator. A defined emotional center trumps the others and gives no clarity in the moment, only clarity over time. Garton, she notes, filters through spleen and sacral to emotional authority. The emotional wave and the 2027 cycle switch Emotional definition, Fletcher says, means living on a wave where a high or a low needs no reason, and the skill is surfing it rather than being crashed around by it. She and Garton share the 37-40 channel running from the emotional center to the ego center, which she calls a ratchet wave that climbs in plateaus then plummets. She contends human design describes roughly 400 year cycles, with the current one switching in 2027 inside the emotional center, and argues emotionally defined people carry the onus of naming their own state honestly. Garton closes by using the system as a diving board into his own intuition.
extra.christopher-mcintosh-occult-germany: Germany's Buried Esoteric Inheritance A German Au Pair and a Lifelong Love Digging for Myths Instead of Bones Barbarossa Asleep Inside the Mountain Why Germans Forgot Their Own Legends The Grail as a Stone from the Stars Nebra Sky Disc and Golden Cone Hats Seidr, the Magic Reserved for Women Spirit and Matter, Hildegard to Steiner Loki, Abraxas and the Union of Opposites Tuisto, Mannus and the German Sky God Takeaways and What's Inside Part Two Amongst the modern trend towards soul suffocating scientific materialism, there remained sparks and embers of a time when our ancestral mind had not yet been forcibly amputated. Chance Garton One of the ways in which this happens is on the level of national heroes, who very quickly turn into figures of mythology. Chance Garton Sleeping Emperors and Mythic Ancestors McIntosh describes the interface between history and myth as a lifelong fascination, noting how national heroes turn into mythical figures almost at once. His German example is the emperor Frederick Barbarossa, said to sleep in a cave in the Kyffhauser range in Thuringia, waking every hundred years to ask a dwarf whether the ravens still circle the mountain. When Bismarck unified Germany in 1871, a huge monument to Wilhelm the First went up there with Barbarossa and a raven at its base. He also traces the older lineage back to Tuisto, cognate with the Sanskrit sky god Dyaus, whose son Mannus fathered three German tribes and gave Mannheim its name. A Country That Forgot Its Own Grail Teaching English at the University of Bremen, McIntosh asked a class what the Holy Grail was, and only one young man ventured that it had something to do with rejuvenation and the quest for eternal life. He calls that a pity, since Wolfram von Eschenbach's Parzival is one of the great medieval epics and Wagner returned to the Grail in Parsifal and Lohengrin. Chance reads the passage where the Grail is not a Christian relic but a stone whose name a heathen read clearly in the constellations. McIntosh offers one speculative theory that the Grail recalls an ancient asteroid crater in what is now the Czech Republic. Vulture Bone Flutes and Golden Cone Hats Against the idea that prehistoric northern Europeans were primitive people without culture, McIntosh points to the Nebra sky disc, which he describes as essentially a lunar calendar probably used for agriculture, and to far older finds: the Venus of Willendorf, a large breasted statuette some 30,000 years old found in Austria in the early twentieth century, and a flute carved from a vulture's bone roughly 35,000 years old. He notes the archaeologist Marija Gimbutas argued such figures evidence an early matriarchal culture in Europe. Chance raises the golden conical hats; McIntosh suggests the cone may serve a purpose similar to a bishop's mitre. Spirituality Brought Down Through the Hands The thread McIntosh calls distinctly German is the marriage of the spiritual with the material. Hildegard of Bingen was an abbess, physician, herbalist, composer and painter whose remedies, he says, were imparted to her in visions, and who repeatedly got into trouble with the church yet argued her way out. Paracelsus wrote as much theology as medicine, Jacob Boehme wrote in alchemical metaphor, and the poet Novalis worked as a mining engineer. Rudolf Steiner, who placed himself in the Rosicrucian line, insisted spirituality be brought into the physical world, yielding homeopathic remedies, biodynamic agriculture, Waldorf schools and eurythmy. Abraxas, Loki and the Union of Opposites Chance argues the deepest thread in Occult Germany is the union of opposites, contending that the church's split of an authorized god of light from a devil produced a sterilizing, anti life force. He cites Hermann Hesse's novel Demian, where Abraxas is both god and devil, and Jung's Seven Sermons to the Dead, where Abraxas is effectiveness itself, a power that non power cannot cancel out. McIntosh agrees that element is suppressed in the Christian scheme and offers Loki, the Nordic trickster who is still part of the universe, the grain of sand in the oyster.

Chance Garton The Blind Spot in Myth Theory Lundwall took his doctorate at Pacifica Graduate Institute, the Joseph Campbell school of comparative myth, and says that eight years of coursework and dissertation writing left him staring at a lacuna: neither Campbell nor Jung, neither Harrison's myth and ritual school nor Eliade's sacred and profane, ever touched orality. He points to two books from the 1960s that reopened the question, Gerald Hawkins' Stonehenge Decoded and Giorgio de Santillana's Hamlet's Mill, both savaged on arrival. Richard Atkinson's rebuttal, titled Moonshine on Stonehenge, insisted the monument was built by howling barbarians. Hawkins, Lundwall notes, turned out to be right. Camps That Followed the Sun Rather than treat sky watching as a curiosity, Lundwall argues that oral peoples organized survival around it. He describes the Lakota, hunter gatherers who broke winter camp for spring camp and then summer camp not simply to chase herds but to follow the sun through their constellations, each camp representing a constellation so the ground carried a sky map while the sky carried a land map. Their original summer camp, he says, was Devils Tower in Wyoming. In the ancient Near East and in Egypt, he adds, you could not build a city until you had first built a temple and cosmicized the land. How Knowledge Survived Without Writing For ninety nine percent of human history there was no writing, so anything worth keeping had to be passed down in memorable form. Lundwall describes oral cultures telling the same knowledge in as many mediums as possible: oral narrative as myth, somatic narrative as dance, ritual timed to a rising sun, a heliacal star rising, or a phase of the moon. Every element in that web, the herd, the valley, the star, the season, gets personified, which is why he contends orality produces polytheism while monotheism is a product of literacy. Deity names, in his reading, work as technical terms, closer to verbs than nouns. Analogy, Orion and the Rain Making Head Oral peoples think analogically, Lundwall argues, and the Pyramid of Unas texts show it. Read glyph by glyph they sound like gibberish, telling you to open the sky door beside the baboon's penis, which one translator renders as the sword of Orion, sitting where the ecliptic crosses the Milky Way. They are not texts at all, he says, but ritual and cosmological scenarios that were danced, sung and chanted. The same logic, he contends, is why Maya and American Southwest cultures tied heads and scalps to rain ceremonies: a head arrives when a woman's water breaks, holds every divine function, and produces tears. Cyclized History and the Flood as Rebirth Because oral societies cannot keep footnoted histories, Lundwall says memory gets cyclized into archetypes of eternal return, and he answers Godfrey Higgins' Anacalypsis puzzle about the absence of history before Herodotus that way. His example is Caribbean vodou, where a village founder's spirit, recalled alongside the Loa, is gradually absorbed into the deity until the historical person is forgotten. He reads the biblical flood as the creation story retold beat for beat, and argues the flood that Utnapishtim recites in the Epic of Gilgamesh is not a clumsy insertion but a resurrection sequence, matching chapter 175 of the Papyrus of Ani.

Matt Presti A documentary aimed at dimensional delusion Chance Garton welcomes back Matt Presti to unpack his film Dispelling Dimensional Madness, a ten year project built from more than two hundred hours of research. Presti argues that belief in higher dimensions is not ancient wisdom but a recent invention traced through spiritualism, scientific romance and academic mathematics. He says the hardest part of making the film was that he could find no other detractors, only papers written by people friendly to the idea. His stated purpose is blunt, to hold people's feet back to the ground and get their heads back into the life they are actually living. Where the fourth dimension actually came from The conversation walks the history in detail. Henry More coined the term fourth dimension in his 1671 Enchiridion Metaphysicum, opposing Cartesian dualism and describing a spiritual substance he called essential spissitude, essentially Plato's realm of ideal forms. Jean le Rond d'Alembert was the first mathematician to fold time in as a fourth dimension. Presti also cites Gerard Hickson's book King's Dethroned, which argues time cannot be a fourth dimension because length, breadth and width are not independent of one another, while Einstein treats his dimensions as if they were. Seances, fraud and the birth of the fifth dimension Presti traces the popular version of higher dimensions to the spiritualist craze of 1850s to 1880s London, which he calls New Age 1.0. Johann Zollner of Leipzig University hired the medium Henry Slade, recommended by Helena Blavatsky, who wrote on a chalk slate with his foot and claimed spirits in the fourth dimension were doing it. Slade was caught, fled Europe and died broke. Sir William Crookes, inventor of the cathode ray tube, was fooled at seances by a woman dressed as a ghost called Katie King while grieving his brother. Escapism, ascension symptoms and honesty Both men separate healthy escape, a walk in the woods or a sitcom, from what Presti calls toxic escapism, the Gnostic sense that this place is a hell hole to flee. Chance pushes back gently on the flat earth example, noting most flat earthers he knows are homesteading rather than waiting for the ice wall. They then criticize ascension cults that rebrand poor health and unprocessed trauma as five dimensional ascension symptoms. Presti invokes Carl Jung, saying wholeness comes from integrating your own noetic darkness, and Chance argues honesty is the actual key to health. Mind as the fulcrum and hermeticism as the alternative The positive case is Walter Russell's cosmology, where light is the one substance and mind is the non dimensional cause. Presti reads from Atomic Suicide by Walter and Lao Russell on everything being three, then extends the point through fulcrums, the door jamb, the guitar bridge, the seesaw, motion always moving on stillness at ninety degrees. Chance connects this to his biofield tuning work and to mind as the mental plane rather than a physical ether. Presti closes by naming himself a hermeticist and telling listeners their own mind is the fulcrum and the savior.

Sunrise light with no sunglasses and no contacts raises cortisol, blood sugar and hormones on schedule. Fire, candles and incandescent bulbs emit no blue, so they never disturbed our ancestors. LEDs, fluorescents and phone screens emit blue alone, telling the body it is noon at eight at night. Jackie says that is why athletes who eat well and train hard still end up tired and pre diabetic. The Sun As Son Of God And The Spiritual Return Raised in a strict Christian home she ran from, Jackie now says the sun is literally the son of God, and that the Bible reads as astrology told as story. Chance Garton runs with it, describing the sun as a fractal creator one step down from source, and connecting Christos, Krishna and the black sun to the light carried inside the body. Jackie credits a Tulum beach trip with downloading her idea for an animal light therapy device. Chance ties her gut and hormone results to Qigong organ clocks he learned from John Monroe, and to grounding and cold exposure.

Mark Steeves A crowdsourced map of a strange country Mark Steeves came on to talk about Esoteric America, the new show he launched with Chad Stemke after recording five episodes before releasing any of them. The premise is that listeners, not experts, should be the guests. Mark tells Chance Garton he can only speak for Connecticut, so he wants local researchers everywhere filling in the map with mounds, native history, Tartaria, colonial history and oddities like the one footed snorkel monster. He points to Andrea breaking down Baudette, Minnesota and Jack Asgard breaking down the Inland Empire as the model for what the show is trying to build. What S.E.E.E.N. actually asks you to do The pamphlet Mark wrote stands for the Synchromistic Exploration of the Ever Expanding Now, and he frames it as a travel guide to wherever you already are. It grew out of his frustration with the Randonautica app, which never worked in an area with no phone service. The kit is a pair of dice, a compass, a map, a notebook and pen, a camera, a backpack and a cup. The cup holds the dice so you can shake them while driving, with odds meaning left and evens meaning right, provoking randomness until you are genuinely lost. Dreamwalking instead of sleepwalking Mark argues that most of us are sleepwalkers and that dreamwalking is the deliberate opposite, a way of waking up to a reality that is always there the way dreams are. He believes the land itself carries an energetic imprint from the people who lived here for thousands of years, and that those layers sit under only four hundred years of newer history like soil turned over by a farmer. You can connect with ancestors who share no genealogy with you, he says, through the dirt, the plants, the animals and the common ground you both stand on. Why the psychedelic push looks suspicious Chance raises the question of why psychedelics are suddenly being moved into pharmaceutical and psychiatric territory, and suggests a hyper materialistic culture is grabbing them as another experience to collect. Mark answers that science is trying to quantify spirituality by breaking plants down into molecules, and speculates the real goal is finding a chemical bridge into augmented digital reality, noting synthetic compounds are easier to program. His stronger claim is that people have it backwards. The experience is in you and the mushroom only activates it. He compares his book to a swing set next to the roller coaster of ayahuasca. Breaking routine, gratitude and omens The practical heart of the conversation is that our problems live inside our routines, so stepping out of the daily pie chart of hours creates room to see them. Mark asks people to set aside real time, express gratitude, and log every object, omen and occurrence, because a pattern surfaces after a few outings. He teaches a walking meditation of matching steps to breath, and describes the drifting state you enter while driving as a doorway to synchronicity. Chance closes with the copy of The Alchemist by Paulo Coelho that reached him in Chicago days after he asked for it.
